The Suez Crisis. In 1956, Egyptian President Gamal Abdel Nasser nationalized the Suez Canal after the United States withdrew funding for the Aswan High Dam, a deliberate assertion of Egyptian sovereignty over the vital waterway. This nationalization prompted a secret military invasion by Britain, France, and Israel who sought to reclaim the vital waterway and topple his regime. The canal had been under joint British-French control since its construction, generating enormous revenues and serving as a strategic artery of global commerce and imperial power projection. Britain and France coordinated a secret invasion plan with Israel, meeting at Sevres in October 1956 to coordinate military action under the pretext of separating Israeli and Egyptian forces. Israel invaded Sinai on October 29 to seize the Gaza Strip and Eilat. Britain and France then bombed Egyptian airfields and landed paratroopers at Port Said. Soviet Premier Nikita Khrushchev threatened nuclear intervention on behalf of Egypt. Simultaneously, U.S. President Eisenhower opposed the invasion diplomatically and through United Nations channels, fracturing the Western alliance. United Nations emergency force troops deployed to maintain a ceasefire. Britain, France, and Israel withdrew by early 1957 without toppling Nasser or reclaiming the canal. The crisis marked the definitive end of European colonialism in the Middle East and established Nasser as the paramount Arab leader, reshaping Cold War alignments and regional politics for decades. Cold War superpowers and international pressure forced a humiliating Allied withdrawal within weeks, marking a dramatic shift in global power and the decline of European colonialism as well as the rise of non-aligned nations in the postwar order.
